To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the distributed database model should include both replicated data and partitioned data, (2) the distributed database should provide location transparency and failure transparency, (3) the distributed database can provide replica transparency, and (4) the distributed database cannot provide concurrency transparency.

(1) the concepts of transaction and consistency can be defined in a distributed system, (2) the programming interface for a distributed database system should provide location transparency (for partitioned data), replica transparency, concurrency and failure transparencies, and (3) these transparencies can be provided by the programming interface if the underlying system provides certain capabilities.

(i) a transaction is a set of operations on data, which must be executed as an indivisible unit, (ii) the data on which the transaction operates may be distributed over a number of sites, (iii) the data may be replicated at multiple sites, (iv) the transaction must preserve consistency of the data on which it operates, (v) the transaction must be atomic, that is, it must be either completely executed or aborted, (vi) the transaction must provide failure transparency
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design of a system that will provide the programmer with the illusion that all the data in the system is stored in a single file at one site, and that all the data accesses are performed in a sequential, atomic, and failure-free manner.
providing a distributed data management system that is both transparent and efficient.
the development and evaluation of techniques for providing data consistency and location transparency in distributed database systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the problem of distributed database systems is not solved yet, and that there is still a long way to go.
a system which provides location transparency, replica, concurrency and failure transparency, and which provides a transaction mechanism, is a good distributed system.
the concepts of transaction and data consistency are not as well understood as they might be.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a distributed database system must provide location transparency, concurrency transparency and failure transparency.

a distributed database system should support a transaction model that provides a consistent view of data to the applications, and that it is possible to provide such a transaction model in a distributed database system.

a distributed database system should provide the following features: (1) a uniform programming interface to all data, whether local or remote, whether replicated or not; (2) a uniform programming model for all transactions, whether local or distributed, whether serial or parallel; (3) the ability to recover from failures of any node in the system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not possible to provide all four transparencies simultaneously.
the concepts of transaction and consistency in distributed systems are not well defined and that the design of a distributed system must be guided by the application domain.

a distributed system should provide the following: (1) a transaction model, (2) a data model that supports the abstraction of files, (3) a programming language that supports the abstraction, and (4) an execution model for the programming language.
